screens.title: Compliance as Code and Automated Auditing
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we will treat compliance as living code rather than a checklist you run once a year. You will learn how CloudTrail captures the audit trail of A P I activity, how AWS Config continuously records resource configurations and evaluates rules, and how Security Hub aggregates findings so teams can prioritize remediation. We will walk through building custom Config Rules, connecting findings into a CI/CD pipeline, and a hands-on scenario validating S3 default encryption. This matters because auditors and customers expect continuous evidence, and automated controls reduce human error and time-to-fix. As you follow each step, notice the practical trade-offs: logs must be centralized and protected, rules need careful scoping to avoid noise, and remediation should follow least-privilege principles. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design an automated compliance flow that detects, reports, and can remediate common misconfigurations. Consider what compliance gaps you already have in your accounts and how a continuous model would change your incident response.

screens.title: What is Compliance as Code?
screens.narratorSegment: Compliance as Code is the practice of expressing policies and controls as executable, version-controlled artifacts that run continuously against your cloud resources. Instead of manual checklists, you describe desired states — encryption enabled, required tags, network segmentation — and implement automated checks that flag deviations. For example, a rule that requires S3 buckets to enable default encryption can be managed like any other code change: reviewed, tested, and deployed. This changes the feedback loop: developers get early feedback in CI, security teams receive continuous findings, and auditors get an auditable trail. A common misconception is that Compliance as Code replaces human judgment; it does not. Automated checks cover mechanical enforcement and monitoring, while humans still assess risk exceptions and contextual decisions. Another important point is scope: rules should be scoped to the correct accounts and resource types to avoid overwhelming teams with irrelevant alerts. In practice you will store rules and remediation playbooks in source control, test them in staging, and promote them through pipelines. How would you start converting one manual audit item into a coded rule in your environment?

content.html:
Core Concept
Compliance as Code — definition

Policies and controls are written, versioned, and executed so compliance becomes continuous and testable.

Analogy
Think of rules as unit tests for cloud configuration. They fail when a resource drifts from its expected state.
Practical pattern
Versioned rules in Git
Test in staging
CI gate checks
Automated remediation
Common misconception: automation removes the need for audits. Reality: automation provides consistent evidence and reduces manual effort, but human review remains essential for exceptions.
Key Takeaway

Treat policies as code so you can test, version, and run them continuously, improving speed and reproducibility.

screens.title: AWS CloudTrail: the audit trail
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CloudTrail records A P I activity and other events, creating a timeline of who did what in your accounts. It captures management events like console sign-ins and A P I calls, and can capture data events such as S3 object access when enabled. For compliance, CloudTrail provides the forensic evidence auditors expect. A recommended practice is to enable CloudTrail in all regions and deliver logs to a centralized S3 bucket in a separate logging account with encryption and restricted access. This prevents tampering and ensures consistent retention policies. A common mistake is enabling CloudTrail but not data events for services where object-level access matters; you may miss critical access information. Another pitfall is scattering logs across accounts or buckets without centralization, which makes incident investigation slow. As a concrete example, if an IAM role is used to change an S3 bucket policy, CloudTrail records the A P I call, the principal, and request details so you can trace the change. How would you structure your logging account and retention to support both audits and incident investigations? AWS CloudTrail: the audit trail means enable cloudtrail across regions and centralize logs so audit trails are complete, encrypted, and tamper-resistant.. In practical terms, what cloudtrail records and why logs must be centralized. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
AWS CloudTrail
Records API and management events and optionally data events like S3 object access for forensic analysis.
Best practice
Send logs to a central, encrypted S3 bucket in a dedicated logging account and enable multi-region logging.
Common mistake
Not enabling data events for S3 or Lambda, which can hide important access activity.
Concrete example
If an IAM role modifies a bucket policy, CloudTrail stores the API call, caller identity, and request parameters so you can trace the change and correlate with Config findings.
Pro tip
Protect the logging account with strict IAM and MFA and use bucket encryption and lifecycle rules for retention.
Key Takeaway

Complete, centralized logs are the foundation for both audits and incident response.

screens.title: AWS Config: record and evaluate
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Config continuously records resource configurations, maintains a historical timeline, and lets you evaluate resources against desired settings via Config Rules. Config builds an inventory that shows how resources change over time, and its rules can be managed or custom. Managed rules offer common checks like blocking public S3 access, while custom rules let you express organization-specific requirements using Lambda evaluations. Config evaluation events are triggered by configuration changes or on a schedule, so you get near-real-time detection of drift. An important nuance is the difference between 'NOT_APPLICABLE' and 'NON_COMPLIANT' states: a rule should return NOT_APPLICABLE when the resource type doesn't match the rule's intent, to avoid noise. For example, a custom rule can inspect an S3 bucket's tags and versioning status and return COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT accordingly. Make sure Lambda execution roles for custom rules have least privilege and that re-evaluation cadence balances timeliness with cost. How would you design a rule to check only production buckets, not every bucket in the account? AWS Config: record and evaluate means use aws config rules to detect drift by comparing recorded configurations with desired settings continuously.. In practical terms, how config tracks resource state and flags non-compliance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
AWS Config flow
Record → Evaluate → Flag. Config records resource state, evaluates rules, and marks resources as compliant or not.
Inventory
Rules
Evaluations
Design tip: Scope rules with tags or resource filters so only intended resources are evaluated. That reduces false positives and keeps teams focused on relevant findings.
Example: Tag + versioning rule
A Lambda-backed custom rule checks that production S3 buckets have Environment: Production and versioning enabled. If neither condition is met, it returns NON_COMPLIANT.
Common mistake
Treating NOT_APPLICABLE resources as failures. Use NOT_APPLICABLE wisely to avoid noise.
Key Takeaway

Custom rules let you encode organizational policy. Scope and least-privilege reduce noise and risk.

screens.title: Custom AWS Config Rule — Lambda example
screens.narratorSegment: Custom Config Rules are commonly implemented as Lambda functions that receive an invoking event, inspect the configuration item, and return a compliance result. The provided Python example demonstrates this pattern: it parses the invoking event, inspects resourceType and tags, and evaluates bucket versioning. In practice you will deploy this Lambda with a role that allows read access to the configuration item and, if necessary, to query supplementary configuration like versioning status. A useful development pattern is to write the Lambda logic locally, add unit tests that simulate Config invoking events, and deploy via your IaC pipeline. A common misconception is that the Lambda must modify resources. It should only evaluate and report; remediation should be a separate, auditable action. For testing, send a mocked event where resourceType equals AWS::S3::Bucket and confirm the Lambda returns COMPLIANT when tags and versioning match expectations. This separation keeps evaluation safe and deterministic. keyIdea.text: Custom rules should evaluate state and report compliance; do remediation in separate, auditable steps.

content.html:
Definition
Lambda-backed Config Rule
The Lambda inspects the invoking event and returns COMPLIANT, NON_COMPLIANT, or NOT_APPLICABLE.
Example code (simplified)
import json

def lambda_handler(event, context):
  invoking_event = json.loads(event['invokingEvent'])
  configuration_item = invoking_event['configurationItem']

  resource_type = configuration_item['resourceType']
  resource_id = configuration_item['resourceId']

  if resource_type == "AWS::S3::Bucket":
    tags = configuration_item.get('tags', {})
    if tags.get('Environment') == 'Production':
      if configuration_item['supplementaryConfiguration']['BucketVersioningConfiguration']['Status'] == 'Enabled':
        compliance_type = 'COMPLIANT'
      else:
        compliance_type = 'NON_COMPLIANT'
    else:
      compliance_type = 'NOT_APPLICABLE'
  else:
    compliance_type = 'NOT_APPLICABLE'

  return {'compliance_type': compliance_type, 'annotation': f"Resource {resource_id} is {compliance_type}"}
Guidance
  • Give the Lambda least privilege—read Config and resource metadata only.
  • Unit-test the handler with mocked invoking events for each state.
  • Keep evaluation separate from remediation for auditability.
Key Takeaway

Implement custom rules as safe evaluators and test them before enabling wide-scope evaluations.

screens.title: AWS Security Hub: aggregate and prioritize
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Security Hub collects findings from services like AWS Config, GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie, then normalizes them into a common format and ranks them for action. This aggregation reduces tool fragmentation and helps teams focus on the highest priority issues. Security Hub also runs automated checks against built-in standards such as the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and PCI controls, giving you a rapid assessment of posture. A typical workflow is: Config flags a non-compliant S3 bucket, Security Hub ingests that finding, and the security team reviews it alongside other findings from threat detection services. A misconception is treating Security Hub as an auto-remediator; its primary purpose is aggregation and prioritization. You can, however, build automation that reacts to Security Hub findings using EventBridge and Lambda to trigger remediation workflows. When configuring Security Hub, ensure account and region coverage aligns with your organization and that findings are routed to ticketing or SOC pipelines for timely action. What priority rules would you apply to reduce alert fatigue? AWS Security Hub: aggregate and prioritize means security hub normalizes findings and maps them to standards so teams can prioritize and act efficiently.. In practical terms, a single pane for findings across services and benchmarks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
Security Hub vs individual services
Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings; individual services detect and generate findings.
Sources
GuardDuty, Config, Inspector, Macie, partners
Standards
CIS, PCI, Foundational Security Best Practices
Workflow example
Config flags non-compliant S3 bucket; Security Hub ingests and maps the finding; SOC triages and assigns remediation; EventBridge can trigger an automated fix if allowed.
Pro tip
Define severity and suppression rules to reduce noise and focus on true positives.
Key Takeaway

Use Security Hub to correlate findings and align them with compliance frameworks for efficient remediation prioritization.

screens.title: Mapping AWS controls to compliance frameworks
screens.narratorSegment: A practical part of Compliance as Code is mapping platform controls to the requirements of common frameworks. For PCI DSS you map controls like access management to IAM policies, encryption of cardholder data to KMS and S3 encryption, network segmentation to VPC and security groups, and continuous monitoring to CloudTrail and Config. HIPAA focuses on protection of ePHI, which maps to access controls, encryption, audit trails, and incident response capabilities available through these services. GDPR emphasizes privacy controls, data minimization, encryption, and the ability to locate and delete personal data. Security Hub includes controls and checks aligned with these frameworks, giving you a starting point for assessments. The important nuance is that cloud services help you achieve responsibilities in the shared responsibility model, but they do not automatically make you compliant. You still need governance, policies, and evidence that controls are correctly configured and operating. As a result, document mappings and retain evidence from Config and CloudTrail to demonstrate compliance during audits. Mapping AWS controls to compliance frameworks means map cloud services and configurations to framework requirements, then automate checks to produce audit evidence.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Integrating compliance into CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating compliance into CI/CD means running checks early so non-compliant infrastructure never reaches production. Use IaC linters, policy-as-code validators, and managed checks in your pipeline. For CloudFormation, tools like CloudFormation Guard or template lints validate templates before deployment. You can add a pipeline stage that invokes Config rule simulation or static checks against templates to catch missing encryption, tags, or insecure network settings. If a stage fails, the pipeline stops and the team fixes the template. A common misconception is that pipeline checks slow down delivery. In fact, catching issues earlier reduces rework and incident response time. For teams that must remediate automatically, consider safe, idempotent actions triggered after human approval. Also ensure pipeline roles have least privilege and that you record the policy decisions and failures in a central log for audit evidence. When designing pipeline gates, prioritize checks that prevent high-risk misconfigurations first. screens.title: Automated remediation with EventBridge and Lambda
screens.narratorSegment: Automated remediation ties detection to a corrective action, typically using EventBridge to listen for findings and Lambda to perform the fix. For example, an EventBridge rule can match Config non-compliance for an S3 bucket and invoke a Lambda that applies BlockPublicAccess or enables default encryption. To keep remediation safe, separate automated fixes into approved playbooks, include logging and change records, and consider human approval for high-impact changes. A common misconception is to remediate immediately without logging or rollback; this can make investigations harder. Instead, log the finding, attempt an idempotent fix, and record the result in Config and CloudTrail. content.html:
Hands-on Activity
S3 default encryption workflow
Follow these steps to create the managed rule and validate buckets.
# Create a non-compliant bucket
aws s3 mb s3://your-unique-bucket-name-noncompliant

# Create a compliant bucket and enable AES256 default encryption
aws s3 mb s3://your-unique-bucket-name-compliant --region YOUR_REGION --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=YOUR_REGION
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket your-unique-bucket-name-compliant --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules": [{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault": {"SSEAlgorithm": "AES256"}}]}'

# Re-evaluate the Config rule if needed
aws configservice start-config-rules-evaluation --config-rule-names s3-bucket-default-encryption-kms
Checks and gotchas
  • Ensure Config is recording S3 resources in the region.
  • Enable Security Hub to see aggregated findings.
  • Wait for Config re-evaluation or trigger it manually for quicker feedback.

Test both failing and passing resources to validate detection and aggregation flow before automating remediation.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing Compliance as Code, certain recurring errors reduce effectiveness. One is the 'set and forget' mentality — rules and mappings must be reviewed and updated as applications and requirements evolve. Another is ignoring non-compliant findings; automated detection is only useful if someone responds. A frequent operational mistake is not enabling data events or not centralizing CloudTrail logs; missing those records undermines investigations. Overly broad IAM permissions for Config or CloudTrail roles introduces risk; apply least privilege and narrow policies for evaluation and logging. Excessive scope in rules can flood teams with low-value alerts; scope rules by tags, accounts, or resource types to keep findings actionable. Finally, avoid coupling evaluation and remediation in a single opaque Lambda; separate detection from corrective action so each is auditable and testable. Following these safety notes produces a reliable, low-noise automation system that auditors and operators can trust. You will learn how CloudTrail captures the audit trail of A P I activity, how AWS Config continuously records resource configurations and evaluates rules, and how Security Hub aggregates findings so teams can prioritize remediation. We will walk through building custom Config Rules, connecting findings into a CI/CD pipeline, and a hands-on scenario validating S3 default encryption. This matters because auditors and customers expect continuous evidence, and automated controls reduce human error and time-to-fix. As you follow each step, notice the practical trade-offs: logs must be centralized and protected, rules need careful scoping to avoid noise, and remediation should follow least-privilege principles. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design an automated compliance flow that detects, reports, and can remediate common misconfigurations. Consider what compliance gaps you already have in your accounts and how a continuous model would change your incident response.

By the end of this chapter you will automate compliance checks, write targeted rules, and integrate findings into your DevOps pipeline. First, you'll learn to use CloudTrail and AWS Config to build a continuous audit and configuration recording foundation. Next, you will implement custom Config Rules using Lambda for organization-specific policies and test them with concrete examples. You will also aggregate and prioritize findings using AWS Security Hub so that teams have a single view of critical risks. Finally, you will map resources to common compliance frameworks and add checks into CI/CD with automated remediation where safe. Each objective includes practical rationale: automating checks reduces manual error, custom rules capture organizational nuance, centralized findings speed response, and pipeline integration prevents non-compliant deployments. You will practice with an S3 encryption scenario that demonstrates detection, reporting, and remediation. Think of these objectives as combined operational tasks and policy design skills you can apply to meet auditors and improve security posture.

This second objectives screen gives more context on how you will demonstrate each skill. For CloudTrail and Config, you will enable cross-region recording and centralize logs in a separate logging account so integrity and access controls are preserved. Each objective is designed for immediate application: you will create a rule, test a non-compliant resource, view the finding in Security Hub, and run a remediation action. This hands-on practice is vital: automation reduces human error and shortens mean time to remediate.

Compliance as Code is the practice of expressing policies and controls as executable, version-controlled artifacts that run continuously against your cloud resources. Instead of manual checklists, you describe desired states — encryption enabled, required tags, network segmentation — and implement automated checks that flag deviations. For example, a rule that requires S3 buckets to enable default encryption can be managed like any other code change: reviewed, tested, and deployed. This changes the feedback loop: developers get early feedback in CI, security teams receive continuous findings, and auditors get an auditable trail. A common misconception is that Compliance as Code replaces human judgment; it does not. Automated checks cover mechanical enforcement and monitoring, while humans still assess risk exceptions and contextual decisions. Another important point is scope: rules should be scoped to the correct accounts and resource types to avoid overwhelming teams with irrelevant alerts. In practice you will store rules and remediation playbooks in source control, test them in staging, and promote them through pipelines. AWS CloudTrail records A P I activity and other events, creating a timeline of who did what in your accounts. When implementing Compliance as Code, certain recurring errors reduce effectiveness. One is the 'set and forget' mentality — rules and mappings must be reviewed and updated as applications and requirements evolve. Another is ignoring non-compliant findings; automated detection is only useful if someone responds. A frequent operational mistake is not enabling data events or not centralizing CloudTrail logs; missing those records undermines investigations. Overly broad IAM permissions for Config or CloudTrail roles introduces risk; apply least privilege and narrow policies for evaluation and logging. Excessive scope in rules can flood teams with low-value alerts; scope rules by tags, accounts, or resource types to keep findings actionable. Finally, avoid coupling evaluation and remediation in a single opaque Lambda; separate detection from corrective action so each is auditable and testable. Following these safety notes produces a reliable, low-noise automation system that auditors and operators can trust. Let's summarize the most important concepts. First, Compliance as Code turns policy into versioned, testable artifacts that run continuously. Second, CloudTrail provides the audit trail of A P I actions and should be centralized and protected to serve as forensic evidence. Third, AWS Config records configurations and supports managed and custom rules that evaluate resource state and flag non-compliance. Fourth, AWS Security Hub aggregates findings and maps them to standards so teams can prioritize remediation. Fifth, integrate checks into CI/CD to shift compliance left and prevent non-compliant infrastructure from deploying. Finally, safe automated remediation uses EventBridge and Lambda, but separate evaluation and remediation and keep roles least-privilege. These ideas combined let you build an auditable, low-noise compliance pipeline. As you apply these concepts, document your mappings, test rule behavior, and keep alerting focused on actionable issues.

Keep three core ideas front of mind. First, logs and configuration histories are your audit evidence — protect and centralize them. Second, rules are specifications; encode them, test them, and scope them so they are meaningful. Third, aggregated findings drive action — use Security Hub and pipeline gates to prioritize and remedy issues. These practices are not optional: they make audits smoother and reduce risk.
